title: Hallucination Detective
goal: Your kid learns that AI can sound sure and still be wrong. They ask two or three AI tools the exact same question, compare the answers, spot where they disagree or make things up, check against real sources, and decide on an answer of their own that they can actually trust.
need: A grown-up's account on two or three AI tools (most are 13+)
A question you really want answered
A notebook or a shared screen to compare answers

academics.subject: Thinking
academics.text: telling a fact from a confident guess

academics.subject: Digital literacy
academics.text: why AI makes mistakes, and how to catch them

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: The trap is treating the first AI answer as the answer. Your job is to sit at the keyboard with them, ask the same question more than once, and make 'how do we know?' the habit.

plan.what: Pick the question, ask the AIs and compare (Steps 1 to 3).
Check the facts and decide (Steps 4 and 5).
Test the answer in real life.

troubleshoot.a: Still check one claim. Agreeing isn't the same as right: they may have learned the same mistake.

troubleshoot.q: One AI says it doesn't know
troubleshoot.a: That's the most honest answer you'll get. Mark it 'unsure'; it's worth more than a confident wrong one.

troubleshoot.q: They want to trust it anyway
troubleshoot.a: Find one wrong or made-up detail together. One clear miss is more convincing than any warning.

lesson.text: AI tools write answers that sound sure, even when they're guessing, and two tools can give two different answers to the same question. Asking more than one, comparing them and checking with real sources is how you find out what's true.
lesson.before: 'The AI said it, so it must be right.'

model.line: Claude and ChatGPT: list the Universal rides by motion sickness.
Combined the two, then asked Google's AI too.
Rode them ourselves. Mom got motion sick.

lesson.modelNote: Neither list was the whole truth. Comparing them gave a rough idea, and riding the rides gave the real answer, at least for our own stomachs.

steps.title: Pick a question
steps.why: The best questions have an answer you can check. Opinions are hard to fact-check.
steps.kid: Your kid picks a question they really want answered, with an answer you can check later, using the Good questions card in the Detective Toolkit at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Help them choose something real: a trip you're planning, an animal fact, a place you'll visit. Real questions make the checking matter.
ask: What do you really want to know?
How could we check the answer?
steps.tip: Ranking, listing and 'how many' questions are great. AIs often disagree on them.

levels.explore: Pick a question about something you can see or visit, with a parent.
levels.develop: Write a question with a checkable answer.
levels.extend: Write a tricky question, like a ranking or a list, that AIs might disagree on.

steps.title: Ask more than one AI
steps.why: One answer can't be checked against anything. Two or three answers can be checked against each other.
steps.kid: Your kid asks two or three AI tools the exact same question, word for word, and saves or copies each answer.
steps.you: Type it for younger kids, and make sure the question is the same in each tool.
ask: Did we ask them all the exact same thing?
Which answer sounds most sure of itself?
steps.tip: Save each answer as you go, with a copy or a screenshot. Ask again later and it might say something different.

levels.explore: Listen while a parent reads two answers out loud.
levels.develop: Ask two AI tools the same question, and save both answers.
levels.extend: Ask three tools, then ask one of them again and see if its answer changes.

steps.title: Compare the answers
steps.why: Where AIs agree is a starting point. Where they disagree is where to look harder.
steps.kid: Your kid puts the answers side by side and marks what's the same, what's different, and anything only one AI says, using the Compare card.
steps.you: Read them together, one line at a time. Point out when the order, the numbers or the groups change from one tool to another.
ask: What do they all agree on?
What does only one of them say?
steps.tip: Look at how the answers are organized too. If each AI invents different categories, they're building the list themselves, not copying an official one.

levels.explore: Find one thing that's the same and one that's different.
levels.develop: Mark every agree, disagree and only-one-says on both answers.
levels.extend: Make a table: each claim, which AIs said it, and how sure they sounded.

steps.title: Spot the bluff, and check it
steps.why: AI can make up details that sound real. Checking with real sources is how you catch them.
steps.kid: Your kid looks for signs of bluffing using the Spot the bluff card, then checks the claims they doubt against real sources from the Real sources card, like an official website or a video.
steps.you: Show them how to find the official source first. Then ask: 'Does this match what the AI said?'
ask: Which claim are you least sure about?
What does the official source say?
steps.tip: Check the claim that matters most, not every word. For rides, that might be which one spins and which one drops.

levels.explore: Look at a picture or video together to check one claim.
levels.develop: Check three claims against a real source, and mark them true, false or unsure.
levels.extend: Find a claim that one AI got wrong, and explain why it might have made the mistake.

steps.title: Decide your own answer
steps.why: The goal isn't to find the best AI. It's to end up with an answer you can trust, and to know why.
steps.kid: Your kid writes their own answer in a notebook: what the AIs said, what they checked, what they decided, and how sure they are.
steps.you: If you can test it in real life, do. Riding the ride, visiting the place or trying the recipe is the best fact-check there is.
ask: How sure are you, and why?
steps.tip: Rate how sure you are: very, a bit, or not at all. 'A bit' is an honest answer when the sources disagree.

levels.explore: Say your answer, and one way you checked it.
levels.develop: Write your answer, what you checked, and how sure you are.
levels.extend: Write what you'd tell a friend who only asked one AI.

conclusion.headline: They know AI can be wrong, and how to check it.
conclusion.text: Pay attention to the next time AI answers a question at your house. If they say 'let's ask another one' or 'where's the official site?', the detective habit has stuck.
conclusion.celebrate: When they catch an AI mistake, say: 'Good catch. You didn't just believe it, you checked.'
extensions: Ask the same AI the same question a week later, and compare its two answers
Ask an AI about your own town, and check what it gets right and wrong
Ask an AI about something that happened this week, and see if it knows, guesses or searches
Plan a family outing with AI help, then check every detail before you go

signs: They ask a second AI before trusting the first
They look for the official source on their own
They say how sure they are, not just what the answer is
makeItReal: Next time your family uses AI to plan something, like a trip, a day out or a recipe, ask two tools the same question together, compare, and check one detail before you go.

fromHome.text: Before a trip to Universal, we asked Claude and ChatGPT to rank the rides by motion sickness, and got two different orders with made-up categories. We combined them and asked Google's AI for a third opinion. Then we rode them ourselves, and I did get motion sick.
